learning_objective: Explain the relationship between the chemical structures of molecules and the relative strength of their intermolecular forces when (i) the molecules are of the same chemical species and (ii) the molecules are of two different chemical species. (3.1.A)
question: Which type of intermolecular force is the only one acting between nonpolar $\mathrm{CH_4}$ molecules in the liquid phase?

options.A: Dipole-dipole interactions
options.B: London dispersion forces
options.C: Hydrogen bonding
options.D: Ion-dipole forces

explanation: CH4 is nonpolar and has no ions or H bonded to N, O, or F, so only London dispersion forces (temporary, fluctuating dipoles) act between molecules.

distractor_notes.A: Requires permanent dipoles; CH4 has none.
distractor_notes.C: Requires H bonded to N, O, or F.
distractor_notes.D: Requires an ion; none is present.

subject: apchem

question: Which substance can form hydrogen bonds between its own molecules?

options.A: $\mathrm{CH_3F}$
options.B: $\mathrm{CH_3OCH_3}$
options.C: $\mathrm{CH_3OH}$
options.D: $\mathrm{CH_3Cl}$

explanation: Hydrogen bonding requires H covalently bonded to N, O, or F. Only CH3OH has an O-H bond.

distractor_notes.A: Hydrogen is bonded to C, not to F; there is no O-H, N-H, or F-H bond.
distractor_notes.B: All H atoms are bonded to carbon, so there is no donor H.
distractor_notes.D: Cl is not N, O, or F, and H is on carbon.

subject: apchem
learning_objective: Explain the relationship between the chemical structures of molecules and the relative strength of their intermolecular forces when (i) the molecules are of the same chemical species and (ii) the molecules are of two different chemical species. (3.1.A)
question: London dispersion forces arise from which of the following?

options.A: Attraction between the permanent partial charges of polar molecules
options.B: Attraction between an ion and the partial charge of a polar molecule
options.C: Sharing of electrons between neighboring atoms in one molecule
options.D: Coulombic attraction between temporary, fluctuating dipoles

explanation: Momentary uneven electron distribution creates a temporary dipole that induces a dipole in a neighbor; the resulting Coulombic attraction is a dispersion force.

distractor_notes.A: This describes dipole-dipole forces.
distractor_notes.C: This describes a covalent bond, which is intramolecular.

subject: apchem
learning_objective: Explain the relationship between the chemical structures of molecules and the relative strength of their intermolecular forces when (i) the molecules are of the same chemical species and (ii) the molecules are of two different chemical species. (3.1.A)
question: When solid NaCl dissolves in water, which interaction attracts an $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ ion to nearby water molecules?

options.A: Ion-dipole force
options.B: Hydrogen bond
options.C: Dispersion force only
options.D: Covalent bond

explanation: The negative (oxygen) end of each water dipole is attracted to the positive ion: an ion-dipole force.

distractor_notes.B: Hydrogen bonds involve H bonded to N, O, or F attracted to a lone pair, not a bare cation.
distractor_notes.C: Dispersion forces exist but are far weaker than the interaction with the full charge.
distractor_notes.D: Water does not share electrons with Na+.

subject: apchem

question: Which noble gas should have the strongest London dispersion forces between its atoms?

options.A: Ne
options.B: He
options.C: Ar
options.D: Xe

explanation: Dispersion forces increase with the number of electrons (polarizability). Xe has the most electrons of the four, and has the highest boiling point (-108 °C).

distractor_notes.A: Fewer electrons, less polarizable.
distractor_notes.C: More polarizable than He and Ne but less than Xe.

subject: apchem
learning_objective: Explain the relationship between the chemical structures of molecules and the relative strength of their intermolecular forces when (i) the molecules are of the same chemical species and (ii) the molecules are of two different chemical species. (3.1.A)
question: Boiling a sample of liquid water at 1 atm primarily requires overcoming which of the following?

options.A: The covalent O-H bonds within each molecule
options.B: Attractions between separate water molecules
options.C: The ionic bonds between H+ and OH- ions
options.D: The nuclear attraction of oxygen for its core electrons

explanation: Vaporization separates molecules from each other (intermolecular forces); the molecules themselves, and their covalent bonds, remain intact.

distractor_notes.A: Intramolecular bonds remain intact when water boils.
distractor_notes.C: Liquid water is molecular, not an ionic solid.
distractor_notes.D: This is not changed by boiling.

options.C: It is a polar molecule, so dipole-dipole forces act between its molecules, unlike 2-methylpropane.

options.A: The H-F covalent bond is stronger than the H-Cl bond, so HF is harder to vaporize.

distractor_notes.A: Boiling does not break the covalent bond.

question: Propane ($\mathrm{C_3H_8}$, M = 44 g/mol) boils at -42 °C and acetaldehyde ($\mathrm{CH_3CHO}$, M = 44 g/mol) boils at 20 °C. Which statement best explains the difference?

options.A: Acetaldehyde has stronger dispersion forces because it has more atoms.
options.B: Acetaldehyde forms hydrogen bonds because it contains oxygen.
options.C: Propane has stronger covalent bonds than acetaldehyde.
options.D: Acetaldehyde is polar, so dipole-dipole forces add to its dispersion forces.

distractor_notes.C: Covalent bond strength is not relevant to boiling.

options.A: Hydrogen bonding between two $\mathrm{H_2O}$ molecules

options.C: Dipole-dipole attraction between two $\mathrm{HCl}$ molecules
options.D: London dispersion forces between two Ne atoms

options.D: Ion-dipole forces

options.A: The N of one molecule and the N of a neighboring molecule
options.B: The H of one molecule and the H of a neighboring molecule
options.C: The N and an H within the same molecule
options.D: The H of one molecule and the N of a neighboring molecule

explanation: The hydrogen bond is an attraction between the partially positive H and the lone pair on the N of an adjacent molecule.

distractor_notes.A: Both are partial negative; they repel.
distractor_notes.B: Both are partial positive; they repel.
distractor_notes.C: That is a covalent bond, not an intermolecular force.

options.A: Covalent bonds between the amino acid side chains of adjacent turns
options.B: Hydrogen bonds between N-H and C=O groups of the backbone
options.C: Ionic bonds between adjacent peptide bonds
options.D: Dispersion forces only, because the backbone is nonpolar

explanation: Noncovalent interactions (CED 3.1.A.5), here hydrogen bonds between backbone N-H and C=O groups, hold regions of one large molecule in a specific shape.

distractor_notes.A: Covalent bonds form the backbone, not the helical turns.

options.A: $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$
options.B: $\mathrm{Li^{+}}$
options.C: $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$
options.D: $\mathrm{K^{+}}$

explanation: Ion-dipole attraction grows with ion charge and shrinks with ion-molecule distance. Mg2+ has a 2+ charge and a small radius, giving the greatest charge density.

distractor_notes.B: Higher charge density than K+ or Na+, but lower than Mg2+.
distractor_notes.C: Only a 1+ charge, so weaker than Mg2+.
distractor_notes.D: Lowest charge density of the four.

question: A student claims: "Br2 is a liquid and I2 is a solid at room temperature because I2 molecules are more polar." Which response best evaluates the claim?

options.A: The claim is correct: iodine is less electronegative than bromine, so I2 has a larger dipole moment.
options.B: The claim is incorrect: Br2 has hydrogen bonding that I2 lacks.
options.C: The claim is correct: dipole-dipole forces explain most halogen properties.
options.D: The claim is incorrect: both are nonpolar, and the larger, more polarizable I2 has stronger dispersion forces.

explanation: X2 molecules are nonpolar; the increase in electrons from Br2 to I2 raises polarizability and dispersion forces, making I2 a solid.

distractor_notes.A: Both are homonuclear and nonpolar, so I2 has no dipole moment.
distractor_notes.C: No halogen molecule X2 has a permanent dipole.

options.A: $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ → $\mathrm{K^{+}}$
options.B: $\mathrm{K^{+}}$ → $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$
options.C: $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ → $\mathrm{Cs^{+}}$
options.D: $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ → $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$

explanation: Ion-dipole attraction strengthens with increasing charge and decreasing size: K+ → Ca2+ raises the charge from 1+ to 2+ at a similar radius.

distractor_notes.A: This is the reverse; charge density decreases.
distractor_notes.D: Lower charge and larger radius reduce attraction.

question: A student argues: "CH4 should boil higher than H2O because CH4 has more atoms per molecule." Which response best evaluates the argument?

options.A: The argument is sound: a greater number of atoms always produces stronger intermolecular forces in a small molecule.
options.B: The argument is flawed: water molecules are nonpolar and therefore attract each other more weakly than methane does.
options.C: The argument is flawed: hydrogen bonding in water produces much stronger intermolecular forces than the dispersion forces in methane.
options.D: The argument is sound: boiling requires breaking covalent bonds, and C-H bonds are weaker than O-H bonds.

explanation: Water has strong hydrogen bonds; methane has only weak dispersion forces, so water has the higher boiling point.

distractor_notes.A: Atom count alone does not set intermolecular strength; hydrogen bonding dominates here.
distractor_notes.B: Water is polar and hydrogen bonds.
distractor_notes.D: Boiling overcomes intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds.

question: Ionic solids are brittle because, when a crystal is struck and one layer of ions shifts,

options.C: covalent bonds between the ions must stretch and break

distractor_notes.B: This describes metallic solids, which are malleable.
distractor_notes.C: Ionic solids have no covalent bonds between ions.
distractor_notes.D: Ionic solids do not contain separate molecules.

question: The molar absorptivity of a species is measured as 1.5 × 10$^4$ L/(mol·cm). Which choice gives the correct units of ε and indicates that absorbance has what units?

options.A: ε has units mol L$^{-1}$ cm, and absorbance has units mol/L.
options.B: ε has units L mol$^{-1}$ cm$^{-1}$, and absorbance has no units.
options.C: ε has no units, and absorbance has units L/mol.
options.D: ε has units L mol$^{-1}$, and absorbance has units cm.

explanation: A = εbc is dimensionless, so ε must have units (L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹) that cancel those of b (cm) and c (mol/L).

distractor_notes.A: Dimensional analysis requires εbc to be unitless.

question: A student claims: "A solution with an absorbance of 0.60 contains twice the concentration of a solution with an absorbance of 0.30, measured in the same cuvette at the same wavelength." Which response best evaluates the claim?

options.A: The claim is not supported: absorbance is inversely proportional to concentration under identical conditions.
options.B: The claim is not supported: absorbance is proportional to the square of the concentration.
options.C: The claim is not supported: absorbance depends only on the wavelength and never on the concentration.
options.D: The claim is supported within the linear range: absorbance is directly proportional to concentration when b and the absorptivity are constant.

explanation: A = epsilon b c, so with b and epsilon fixed, doubling A means doubling c, valid within the linear range.

distractor_notes.A: A = epsilon b c is direct.
distractor_notes.C: Concentration is in the Beer-Lambert expression.

question: A student wants to build a Beer-Lambert calibration curve for a colored solution. At which wavelength should the absorbances of the standards be measured to give the greatest sensitivity?

options.A: At a wavelength where the solution absorbs essentially no light, since the baseline is flat there.
options.B: At a wavelength chosen at random for each standard so that errors average out over the series.
options.C: At the wavelength of maximum absorbance for the species.
options.D: At the wavelength of the lowest absorbance so that the readings stay below 0.1 for every standard.

explanation: The largest molar absorptivity gives the largest change in A per unit concentration, so measure at the absorbance maximum, keeping the wavelength constant.

distractor_notes.A: No absorption means no usable signal.
distractor_notes.B: The same wavelength must be used for every standard.
